值得閱讀的理由

  • 揭露避難所中常被忽視的女性生理需求與衛生困境，打破官方物資分配的思維盲點。
  • 深入探討日本重大災難後避難所頻繁發生的性暴力與性騷擾黑歷史，剖析體制與社會觀念上的缺失。
  • 提供具體實用的防災應急包整理建議，提醒大眾在防災時兼顧生存與個人尊嚴。

摘要

避難包裡被遺忘的必需品與女性避難困境

主持人范琪斐指出，日本內衣品牌調查顯示僅少數人在防災包中準備了備用內衣，突顯出避難所長年忽略女性生理需求的問題。慶應大學學生表早紀在經歷熊本大地震志工經驗後，研發出專為災民設計的免洗、快乾且具隱蔽性的防災專用內衣，試圖解決避難所缺乏隱私、無法清洗衣物而導致婦科感染的窘境，同時也避免女性曬內衣時面臨被窺視或偷竊的恐懼。

僵化官僚與缺乏女性視角的防災體系

然而這項善意在推廣時卻遭遇體制阻礙。在能登半島地震期間，學生團體嘗試捐贈內衣，卻因官方堅持「齊頭式平等」以及防災官員多為男性、不理解女性生理用品需求等原因，導致內衣無法及時列入官方物資清單。在極端氣候與斷水困境下，災區甚至耗費數週才提供洗衣與沐浴設施，使女性面臨長達一個月無法更換清潔內衣的嚴峻環境。

避難所不能說的秘密：被隱瞞的性暴力陰影

更嚴重的問題在於避難所頻繁發生的性犯罪。從1995年阪神大地震、2011年311大地震到近期的能登與熊本災區，皆發生過管理幹部以物資脅迫女性提供性服務、體育館暗處襲擊、或善心收留卻遭侵犯的案件。過去媒體為了維持「一切安好」的正向氛圍而避而不談，加上受害者在熟人社會的壓力下往往不敢求助，使得避難所的安全隱患不斷重演。

法規演進與民間自救：守護災民尊嚴與安全

儘管日本內閣已於《男女共同參畫基本計畫》中要求納入性別觀點與預防性暴力措施，但社會仍常出現檢討受害者的言論。面對官方防護網的不足，民間組織已主動展開自救，於災區成立專案小組，提供緊急避孕藥與法律諮詢。范琪斐最後提醒，防災不應只著眼於維持生命，更要捍衛災民的個人尊嚴，建議大家可將汰換的舊內衣洗淨放入避難包，作為實用且兼顧衛生的防災備品。

It features quick-drying, easy-washing, and free-size, with. special processing that prevents odors even after three or four days of wear, plus a discreet design. Why does it need to be discreet? Because in shelters, women have to worry about their underwear being stolen or stared at just by hanging it out to dry. This highlights the long-standing issue that Japanese shelters fail to incorporate women's needs into their designs, with the most severe consequence being frequent sex crimes. After the Kumamoto earthquake in July this year, victims complained about the inability to change clothes in shared spaces; one. woman woke up to a stranger staring at her, and requests for partitions were denied, with some victims even living in the same shelter as their neighbors, making it harder to speak out. earthquake and found that shelters were severely lacking in sanitary products and underwear, but everyone was afraid of being judged for making such private requests. Later, when Saki Omote was in college and couldn't attend classes due to the pandemic, she decided to turn the pain points she witnessed into action,. successfully developing the emergency-specific underwear during her junior year. She originally thought a good product would be enough to help, but unexpectedly, she hit a wall with Japan’s rigid system. During the 2024 Noto earthquake, she wanted to donate the underwear to the disaster area, but was told that supplies must be distributed "equally," but since the male-to-female ratio in each shelter varies, how can that be fair? She later tried collaborating with local governments, only to discover an even bigger problem: disaster prevention staff are predominantly male and, being unaware of women's physiological needs, find it difficult to assess the. required quantities of such supplies. Residents complained that shelter toilets were too foul to use.

due to water outages; they dared not drink water, let alone bathe. The city didn't install bathing facilities at the shelters until two weeks after the earthquake. A family kindly let a stranger spend the night in their car, only for him to assault their daughter. While a few men were caught and convicted, it was shocking to find that the perpetrator was a local. (Incoherent segment/text fragment) Japan began focusing on sexual violence in shelters after the 3.11 Great East Japan Earthquake, when many such cases were reported. Some men abused their leadership positions in shelters, demanding sexual favors from. vulnerable women in exchange for supplies; if they refused, they got nothing—forced to choose between starvation or assault. A public health nurse in the disaster zone stated that victims had reported cases of sexual assault and harassment at that time. For instance, many shelters were in gymnasiums where supplies were stored behind stages—blind spots where perpetrators could lure victims under the guise of needing help.

Furthermore, walking to the restrooms from the gymnasium was risky; women going alone risked being groped or even peeping-tom incidents, with problems occurring endlessly. At the time, the representative of the Kobe Women's Support Center urged the media to report on these shelter safety issues, but reporters insisted on focusing only on positive news. This "everything is fine" mentality meant few knew about these events from the Hanshin earthquake, leaving systemic design. flaws unaddressed and causing tragedies to repeat themselves. in their evacuation guidelines, though there is still a long way to go. 值得閱讀的理由

  • 揭露新型求職詐騙陷阱：詳細剖析詐騙集團在LinkedIn等專業社群上偽造職缺與招募人員的常見手法，幫助求職者避免落入圈套。
  • 認識民間網路偵探的奮鬥歷程：介紹「檔案糾察隊長」傑瓊斯在失業困境中，如何憑藉一己之力查出近6萬個假職缺，展現驚人的堅持與社會責任感。
  • 解析求職詐騙背後的心理操縱與龐大損失：探討近年求職詐騙損失暴增五倍的現況，以及詐騙者如何利用「招聘愛情轟炸」與求職焦慮進行心理操縱。

摘要

網路求職陷阱多：「檔案糾察隊長」橫空出世

作者指出，在求職市場競爭激烈的情況下，許多求職者收到知名大企業的面試通知往往欣喜若狂，但這些工作機會與招募人員很可能完全是虛假的。美國男子傑瓊斯（Jay Jones）近年化身為求職平台的網路偵探，自稱檔案糾察隊長（The Profiler），專門追查各類假帳號與假職缺，至今已揪出將近6萬個假職缺，甚至揭露跨國大企業徵才頁面遭詐騙集團利用的驚人事實。

拆解三大求職詐騙手法：假帳號、盜身分與假職缺

瓊斯歸納出三種常見手法：第一是「假帳號假身份」，詐騙者大量複製虛構履歷顧問或招募人員檔案，主動接洽求職者，並以「修改履歷才能獲錄取」為由收取數百至上千美元，或藉背景調查騙取駕照與社安碼後封鎖失聯；第二是「真帳號假身份」，盜用已通過平台驗證但久未上線的真實用戶帳號，改造成假招募人員以博取信任；第三是「真公司假職缺」，如在知名汽車品牌的官方頁面張貼多筆內含外部惡意連結的假職缺，藉由大眾對名企的信賴行騙。

遭逢裁員困境卻堅持打詐：傑瓊斯的奮戰與困境

令人感佩的是，瓊斯並非資安專家，原本只是一名廣告文案寫手。他在女兒出生前兩週突遭公司無預警裁員，面對龐大生活壓力上網求職時，卻屢屢撞見詐騙集團趁火打劫，憤而決定投入查證工作。雖然他協助平台移除了大量詐騙廣告，成了打擊詐騙的小有名氣人物，但他自身卻面臨窮到剩不到200美元、繳不出房租與車貸的窘境，只能靠開Uber與募款苦撐養家，但他仍期盼自己的行動能為孩子樹立挺身對抗不公的榜樣。

求職詐騙金額暴增與平台機制的防範死角

美國官方數據顯示，求職與假仲介詐騙造成的年度損失在數年間從9000萬美元飆升至超過5億美元。詐騙者常利用裁員造成的PTSD及焦慮，對求職者進行「招聘愛情轟炸（recruiting love bombing）」以攻破心防。雖然平台宣稱運用AI加強防詐與審核，但受害者檢舉下架的流程繁瑣費時，往往在詐騙得手後平台才反應過來，這也讓越來越多網友呼籲平台應正視漏洞，甚至聘用瓊斯來改善防護機制。

=============

如果你已經失業好幾個月，每天在網路上投履歷，好不容易收到一封面試通知，對方還是知名大企業，是不是會很開心？但這份工作恐怕從頭到尾都是假的。美國有個叫傑瓊斯（Jay Jones）的男子，近年開始當起求職平台的網路偵探，專門追查假職缺、假招募人員。幾年下來，瓊斯已經追查出將近6萬個假職缺，甚至連知名企業的徵才頁面，都被他查出遭到詐騙集團利用。他是怎麼辦到的呢？我們來認識這位「檔案糾察隊長」傑瓊斯。

網路求職陷阱多：「檔案糾察隊長」橫空出世

作者指出，在求職市場競爭激烈的情況下，許多求職者收到知名大企業的面試通知往往欣喜若狂，但這些工作機會與招募人員很可能完全是虛假的。美國男子傑瓊斯（Jay Jones）近年化身為求職平台的網路偵探，自稱檔案糾察隊長（The Profiler），專門追查各類假帳號與假職缺，至今已揪出將近6萬個假職缺，甚至揭露跨國大企業徵才頁面遭詐騙集團利用的驚人事實。

拆解三大求職詐騙手法：假帳號、盜身分與假職缺

瓊斯歸納出三種常見手法：第一是「假帳號假身份」，詐騙者大量複製虛構履歷顧問或招募人員檔案，主動接洽求職者，並以「修改履歷才能獲錄取」為由收取數百至上千美元，或藉背景調查騙取駕照與社安碼後封鎖失聯；第二是「真帳號假身份」，盜用已通過平台驗證但久未上線的真實用戶帳號，改造成假招募人員以博取信任；第三是「真公司假職缺」，如在知名汽車品牌的官方頁面張貼多筆內含外部惡意連結的假職缺，藉由大眾對名企的信賴行騙。

求職詐騙金額暴增與平台機制的防範死角

值得閱讀的理由

  • 了解特斯拉 Roadster 展示的驚人特技，以及讓車輛短暫飛起來的技術構想。
  • 看懂這款車距離真正量產、上路與日常使用，仍有哪些安全、價格和法規障礙。
  • 從 Roadster 的發表看見特斯拉、中國車廠與全球汽車產業競爭方向的轉變。

摘要

飛天 Roadster 震撼登場

作者介紹，特斯拉在德州 SpaceX 火箭測試基地展示第二代電動跑車 Roadster。白色跑車衝上近乎垂直的斜坡，倒掛在軌道上，接著翻轉落地，最後以噴射推進方式躍過一排汽車。現場投資人與科技創作者看得目瞪口呆，甚至有人懷疑畫面是否由 AI 製作；馬斯克則表示，目標是在 2028 年投入生產。

從電動跑車到極限工程展示

第一代 Roadster 在 2008 年問世，證明電動車也能成為高性能跑車；第二代則早在 2017 年公布，原定 2020 年交車，歷經多次延宕後才迎來這次展示。作者引述參與研發的前特斯拉工程師回憶，馬斯克曾要求團隊打造能倒著行駛、甚至飛起來的跑車，工程師便將計畫戲稱為「最瘋狂的展示」。

影片提到，展示所用的兩項技術，一是車底的強力風扇，藉由抽走車底空氣形成壓力差，讓車身吸附於軌道；二是借用 SpaceX 的氣體推進器，將高壓氣體朝不同方向噴出，以反作用力推動車輛。特斯拉並宣稱 Roadster 從靜止加速至每小時 96.6 公里只需 0.8 秒。不過，這次展示的飛行能力仍有限，車輛只能短暫離地，並非能持續飛行的交通工具。

離大眾上路仍有距離

展示車內沒有駕駛，工程團隊指出高壓氣體系統仍具危險性，馬斯克也坦言，為避免受傷甚至死亡風險，示範時沒有安排真人駕駛。多家媒體因此質疑，這究竟是可實際購買的產品，還是一次吸睛的工程表演。Roadster 的交付時間已從原先承諾延至 2028 年；續航數據也從早年宣稱的超過 1,000 公里，下修至約 480 公里。

作者指出，一般性能版本的訂金約為新台幣 162 萬元；真正具飛行能力的「火箭版」僅有一個座位、採邀請制，也不能在公共道路行駛。即使技術成熟，現行道路與航空法規也未必允許車輛在道路上起飛或降落。美國相關單位對它應如何歸類尚無明確答案，州政府是否准許車輛飛越道路，也仍是待解問題。

特技背後的產業競爭

部分分析人士認為，這場展示主要是展現工程實力、吸引目光，未必代表產品已具備商業化條件；對投資人而言，獲利能力與現金流仍比炫目的飛車畫面重要。作者也提到，Roadster 可能象徵特斯拉與 SpaceX 技術整合的想像，而特斯拉近年逐漸將重心轉向自動駕駛、AI 與機器人。馬斯克更表示，Roadster 將是特斯拉最後一款主要為人類駕駛者設計的新車。

《華爾街日報》所引述的觀點則認為，這場活動也反映特斯拉面對中國電動車競爭時，正試圖把戰場移往更具差異化的領域。影片指出，中國車廠在製造成本、軟體開發與推出新車的速度上具有優勢；馬斯克過去也警告，若沒有關稅或貿易壁壘，中國車廠可能重創全球其他汽車公司。Roadster 作為旗艦車款，則能讓特斯拉再次展現其工程形象，提醒市場它曾是電動車革命的領頭者。

飛行車會成為下一個戰場嗎？

作者提到，中國車廠人士看過展示後也給予肯定，但同時指出飛行安全、續航能力與法規認證仍是關鍵。整體而言，特斯拉能打造令人驚豔的展示車，並不等於能量產出多數人買得起、用得上的產品。隨著車廠競爭延伸至 AI、機器人、自動駕駛與低空經濟，飛行車可能成為下一個產業戰場，而中國也將參與其中。作者最後邀請觀眾思考：飛行車何時才能普及，人們又是否願意親自駕駛。

================================================

Have you ever fantasized while stuck in traffic that you could just fly your car over the vehicles ahead? Things that only happen in sci-fi movies might now become reality, because last week, Musk's Tesla actually showcased a flying car. At the launch event, this sports car flipped upside down and even took off from a standstill, stunning the investors present. Musk even announced plans for production by 2028, so is a future filled with flying cars. really upon us? A high-altitude, groundbreaking, and revolutionary invention. Last week, Tesla unveiled its second-generation electric sports car, the Roadster, at the SpaceX rocket testing base in Texas. The venue lights dimmed, smoke filled the air, and a countdown began as a white sports car suddenly charged straight toward an L-shaped ramp. Unexpectedly, the car not only climbed upward, ignoring the 90-degree vertical slope, but in the end, it even stuck upside down onto the track. That wasn't all; the next second , the car launched off the ramp,. flipped 180 degrees in mid-air, landed steadily on four wheels, and finally, performed a jet-powered takeoff, leaping over a whole row of cars. According to Reuters, the audience was left dumbfounded. One Tesla investor said it was the craziest product demo he had ever seen, and despite being there in person, he couldn't help but wonder: is this really not AI? Another tech investor also remarked that the video looked exactly like a science fiction movie. Tech YouTubers are questioning: can Tesla really manage to mass-produce flying cars by 2028? So,.

how exactly did Tesla make the car fly? Let's first talk about the background; the Roadster actually holds a very special significance for Tesla. In 2008 , Tesla launched the first-generation Roadster, proving that electric vehicles don't have to be slow commuting tools but can also be high-performance sports cars. The second-generation Roadster was announced back in 2017. At the time, Musk claimed its performance would once again disrupt the automotive industry. It was originally expected to ship in 2020, but with repeated delays, it took nearly nine years to finally reach this launch event. The R&D story behind it. is even more cinematic. The British newspaper The Times interviewed former Tesla engineer Kruck, who participated in the development. He recalled that Musk gathered a group of engineers last year, demanding they build a sports car that could drive upside down and also fly. The engineers were stunned, wondering how they would ever pull it off, so the team simply nicknamed the project "The Craziest Demo Ever." Ultimately, they accomplished the challenge using two key technologies. The first was installing powerful fans in the chassis to extract air from beneath the car, using pressure. differences to keep the vehicle firmly suctioned to the ground, allowing it to even drive upside down. The second was borrowing gas thrusters from SpaceX. This technology can eject high-pressure gas in different directions, using reaction force to propel the vehicle, much like a balloon that shoots off in the opposite direction when you let it go. With these technological breakthroughs, Tesla claims the second-generation Roadster can accelerate from zero to 96.6 km/h in as little as 0.8 seconds. Crocker recalled that when the engineers first succeeded in getting the car to drive upside down.

, the entire team cheered and hugged in excitement. But don't think you'll be commuting in a flying Tesla tomorrow, because the car can currently only lift off briefly; it is not yet a vehicle capable of sustained flight. Furthermore, there was no one inside the demonstration car at the launch event. The engineering team revealed that the high-pressure gas system is still dangerous, and even Musk admitted that they didn't use a human driver to avoid the risk of injury or even death. But does this mean we have a long wait. before flying cars can hit the road? Regarding this question, we can look at the reactions from international media. Although they acknowledge that Tesla's technology demonstration was incredibly impressive, many question whether this flying car is just a gimmick or a finished product that the public can actually drive. For example, the US tech media outlet The Verge stated bluntly that while the demo was spectacular, it was essentially just a performance. There are several reasons for this. First, the car was unveiled in 2017 with promises of delivery by 2020, but it has now been pushed back to 2028. Also, the 2017 claim of over. 1,000 kilometers of range has shrunk to about 480 kilometers in the figures released this time, which is a bit of a letdown. Furthermore, although Tesla has reopened pre-orders, Reuters reports that the standard performance version requires a deposit of about 1.62 million NT dollars. The "Rocket" version, which actually has flight capabilities, not only has one seat and is available by invitation only, but it is also not permitted on public roads. This means consumers cannot currently buy the full flight-capable version shown; mass production is at least two.

years away. Thus, experts point out that this is just a special display vehicle built with existing technology and may not necessarily reach the road. Even setting aside technical issues, legal frameworks are likely to lag behind flying car technology. For instance, CBS asked regulators, and even the U.S. Department of Transportation doesn't know if this vehicle can actually be driven on the road. The FAA stated that the demo vehicle doesn't fit the definition of an aircraft, but that doesn't mean it can legally fly over roads. General vehicles must follow road safety. regulations, and states may restrict vehicle takeoffs and landings. Legal scholars are asking: would state governments really allow someone stuck in traffic to suddenly take flight? So, this flying car likely has a long regulatory process ahead before it can hit the road. Therefore, the main purpose of this "flying show" is simply to grab headlines. An asset management firm described the launch as nothing more than a display of engineering prowess; beyond embarrassing traditional automakers, it has almost no commercial value. Analysts also remind us that for investors, a company’s profit margins and cash. flow data are far more important than spectacular visuals of a flying car. However, some analysts believe what the event really aimed to showcase was the potential for future integration between Tesla and SpaceX. Reuters pointed out that Tesla has gradually shifted its focus in recent years toward autonomous AI and robotics, even halting sales of the Model S and Model X to pour resources into humanoid robots. Musk also said the Roadster will be Tesla’s last new car model primarily designed for human drivers.

Why would Musk spend so much effort building a flying car that might never be mass-produced? But perhaps. The Wall Street Journal noted that what this event really reveals isn't how much Musk wants cars to fly, but rather that as Chinese EVs get more impressive, Tesla must gradually withdraw from traditional automotive competition. Let’s look at some data here: according to research from an international consulting firm, the average manufacturing cost of a Chinese-brand EV is about NT $ 650,000, while a comparable European car costs. around NT $ 1.01 million. Chinese automakers also hold an advantage in software development and the speed of launching new models. At this year's Paris Motor Show, the number of Chinese brands grew from nine two years ago to about 20. That’s why, as early as 2024, Musk publicly warned during a Tesla earnings call that without tariffs or trade barriers, Chinese automakers would likely crush most other car companies in the world. Consultants who have long studied China's auto industry believe that China's manufacturing capability continues to drive down costs, forcing. Western automakers to increase their product value; otherwise, they may be phased out and forced to focus only on specific niche markets in the future. The Roadster is a flagship model. Auto analysts at Chenxin Company point out that Tesla currently lacks a luxury performance car to showcase its engineering prowess, and the Roadster can fill that void. In other words, Musk wants to remind everyone why Tesla was once considered the leader of the electric vehicle revolution. This move is quite effective, as some Chinese automakers were also surprised after watching this launch event. According.

to China's Daily Economic News, the founder of NIO publicly praised Tesla after watching the video, even saying, "We really don't have this." The founder of XPeng said it is a cool flying car, but its real-world application still depends on flight safety, range, and whether it can pass relevant legal certifications. Looking back, this launch event also reflects a major transformation taking place in the global automotive industry. In the past, Tesla relied on EV technology to lead traditional automakers. But as Chinese manufacturers outperformed them in battery production costs and mass. production speed, Musk had to shift the battlefield to AI, robotics, autonomous driving, and even combine space tech to launch extreme products. However, being able to create an impressive demonstration and being able to make products that most people can afford and actually use are two different things. That said, flying cars will likely become the new battlefield for the auto industry, and China will certainly be part of this game. Following Tesla's launch, concepts related to flying cars and the low-altitude economy in the Chinese stock market surged. We welcome. everyone to discuss: how long do you think it will be before the flying cars Musk introduced this time are seen everywhere? Would you like to drive a flying car like this?
